text: Fifty-one minutes of finished film, and the assembly of them took ten years. From a house at Rolle, Godard cut fragments of other people's pictures against paintings, photographs, music and voices reading aloud, and this first installment is where the method declares itself. Nothing is explained. Images arrive, break off, return later with a different sound laid under them, and the argument, which is an argument about an entire art, is made in the joins rather than in sentences. The demand it places on a viewer is unusual and unconcealed: recognition at a glance, of images that come in pieces, sometimes for less than a second. Sight & Sound's critics have voted it onto their poll. Melancholy runs through the whole thing openly, and so does a plain tenderness toward the material being taken apart.

The boy's account of his own conception involves a crate of Sicilian tomatoes and an accident. He is not joking, and the film takes him at his word; that is the whole of its method. Around him a French-speaking Canadian household goes about its ordinary business, and the ordinariness is what does the damage. Against it, an imaginary Italian father is the one fact about his life he has been able to choose. Jean-Claude Lauzon keeps comedy, fantasy and plain domestic misery inside a single frame with no seam between them, which is why a summary of the plot and the experience of watching produce two different films. TIFF counts it among the ten best pictures Canada has made. The tomato is not a gag the movie tells about the boy. It is his, and he keeps it.

A family walks, and the country they are crossing offers no reason to stop and nothing to stop for. Nelson Pereira dos Santos filmed Vidas Secas in the dry northern interior with a documentary's patience: hard flat light, long distances, speech rationed down to what people say when talking costs energy. The drama is arithmetic. Water, work, the animals, the number of days to the next place. Nothing is arranged to make hardship legible to a visitor; the camera stays at the height of the people in it and lets the land be exactly as large as it is. Abraccine's hundred best Brazilian films includes it, which means Brazil files this under its own account of itself rather than under somebody else's idea of the badlands. A hundred minutes, and much of what happens is weather.

The marriage takes almost no time to decide and the rest of the film to live in. She is Lithuanian and the war has just ended, which is explanation enough for saying yes to a stranger; he is from Stromboli, and going home means bringing her to an island where everyone has known everyone since birth. What follows is not a quarrel but an accumulation: a language she does not have, a routine set by other people's weather and other people's custom, the particular exhaustion of being looked at all day by neighbours who have not yet decided about her. Rossellini supplies no villain, which makes the situation harder rather than gentler. Italy keeps the picture on its register of films worth saving. A hundred and seven minutes on how much of an afternoon's decision a person can be held to.

The money arrives with no name attached, and that is the trap. An orphan is told by a lawyer that someone unseen intends to make him a gentleman, and the offer is taken up long before anybody asks what will be owed for it. Lean's Dickens runs under two hours, which for this novel means ruthlessness: years vanish in a cut, and what survives the compression is the machinery of a single grudge, an old woman who never left the day she was jilted and the girl she raised for the express purpose of being cold. The black-and-white photography took an Academy Award and earns it indoors, where daylight enters that house like a concession. Pip's real education is in embarrassment. Rising in the world, the film notices without ever saying so, means learning to be ashamed of the people who fed him.

A charity parade needs vehicles, so the man with the three-wheeler is hired for the day. The scheme he has been hired into is a Christmas entertainment in which the town's well-off ladies each take a poor man home to their own table, one seat per household, dinner at the appointed hour. Plácido has a day of his own to get through, and it keeps being interrupted by the timetable of other people's goodness. Eighty-four minutes, and the shortness works as pressure: obligations multiply faster than the hours do. Luis García Berlanga arranges things so that nobody is quite a hypocrite and nothing goes cleanly. The ladies mean it, the poor men are on a schedule, and the machinery grinds anyway. Caimán's hundred best Spanish films has room for it. It is funny the way a queue is funny, from inside.

Two boys grow up on the same land, one in the family that owns it and one in the family that works it. The twentieth century then arrives to make that difference into a matter of sides. Bertolucci gave the story five hours and seventeen minutes, which is not indulgence but a proposition: that an arrangement between classes changes very slowly and then breaks all at once, and that a film about it should be built at the pace of the slow part. What the length buys is intimacy at enormous scale. Every political turn lands as a private debt or a private betrayal, because the faces carrying it have been on screen since childhood. Its account of fascism has been argued with in print ever since, which is a kind of respect; nobody bothers to argue with a film that has decided nothing.

The underworld word for what Chas Devlin does is performing: the trade of frightening people until they agree. Turner is a rock star who has stopped going out. When the film puts the two of them in the same rooms, the pun in the vocabulary becomes the actual subject, two occupations that run on the management of other people's attention and fear, only one of them illegal. Nicolas Roeg cuts in fragments, sliding between the men until it is no longer obvious whose room, or whose memory, is on screen. It begins as a crime picture and does not stay one. The BFI keeps it among a hundred British films, where it sits oddly. The discomfort it produces is engineered rather than accidental, and a hundred and six minutes is long enough for it to become the point.

The subject is not a film but the making of one, watched while it is still happening. For forty-four minutes Hans-Dieter Hartl points a camera at the production of Berlin Alexanderplatz, the German television serial of 1980, and attends to the labour rather than the result: the hours a scene takes before it becomes a scene, the waiting that is most of the work. Documents like this are normally made to accompany a release and discarded afterward. This one is on Die wichtigsten deutschen Filme. There is a specific interest in seeing an enormous production while it is still only effort, because nothing yet carries the authority of a finished image, everyone on the floor is guessing, and the decisions being taken will look inevitable only later.

The trip is paid for by a drug deal, and after that there is nothing to do but ride east. Wyatt and Billy call it a search for spiritual truth; the film neither endorses the phrase nor laughs at it, and mostly keeps two men and two Harleys in frame while the country goes past. Ninety-six minutes is brisk for a road picture, so America arrives in fragments and each stop has to make its point fast, which suits a film whose real business is how strangers get received. Dennis Hopper directs and rides. It is in the National Film Registry, and it has been absorbed so completely into its own imagery that the object itself is easy to overlook: long stretches with nobody talking, and a mood that shifts the moment the engines stop.

A lecture that keeps interrupting itself to stage the thing it is explaining. The thesis, put forward in 1922, is that the women tried as witches in the Middle Ages were suffering what the clinics of Christensen's own day were diagnosing as hysteria, and the evidence is not tabulated but performed: grave robbing, torture, possessed nuns, a Sabbath attended in full. The scholarly frame turns out to be a permit. It lets the director film everything the frame officially deplores, at length, and the result runs from clinical to obscene to broadly comic, sometimes inside one sequence. FLM's list of the best Swedish films includes it. A hundred and five silent minutes in which the demons are handmade, visibly so, and are worse for it.

The case is a missing person, and the detective is in no condition to keep notes. Los Angeles at the turn of the 1970s is both the setting and the obstacle: everyone Doc talks to knows something adjacent, nobody quite lies, and information arrives faster than he can file it. Paul Thomas Anderson lets the mystery run two and a half hours without ever tightening it into something that could be recited back, and the looseness is the design rather than a failure of it. The comedy is played straight, in long scenes of two people talking slightly past each other with the camera declining to help. The BBC has it among the hundred best films of this century. What holds it together is not plot but the sound of a decade closing: paranoia treated as ordinary weather, and a man doing his job inside it anyway.

A ruler consolidating power against his aristocracy and his closest friends, filmed in the Soviet Union in 1944. The manner is closer to opera than to chronicle, and that was precisely the trouble: the production overran its costs and used techniques the producer had forbidden, which is how a three-part life of Ivan IV became one released film, a second held back until a decade after Eisenstein's death, and a third stopped in its earliest days of shooting. He made nothing after it. Ninety-five minutes of court arithmetic, who is owed and who is watching and who has changed sides this week, carried almost entirely by faces held longer than a story requires. The scale is enormous and the drama is claustrophobic, and the combination appears to be deliberate.

Ten years after the events, the October Revolution was restaged for the camera in the country it had produced. That circumstance governs everything: the crowds are re-enactors, the tone is celebratory, and the question of what happened was settled long before the first shot. The reason to watch is the cutting. Eisenstein builds the film so that meaning sits in the join between two images rather than inside either one, an object against a face, a gesture against a statue, sequences that argue where they might have narrated. Following a plot is not really the activity on offer. A hundred and fifteen minutes of a persuasion machine running at full power, and the odd pleasure of watching the mechanism work while remaining unpersuaded by it.
